Minimum Risk Point Estimation of a Mean, Distribution Free

Source: R/seq_mr_dfr_mean_arb.R
seq_mr_dfr_mean_arb.Rd

Given the data collected so far, checks the stopping rule of the purely sequential minimum risk point estimation (MRPE) procedure for a population mean when the distribution is not specified and the variance is unknown and unrestricted (Mukhopadhyay and de Silva, 2009). Estimation error and sampling both cost something; the procedure looks for the sample size at which their expected total, the risk, is smallest. That sample size depends on the unknown variance, so observations are collected until the sample size reaches the size the current estimate calls for. The procedure is risk based, so there is no confidence level.

Usage

seq_mr_dfr_mean_arb(x, A, c, gamma = 1, na.rm = TRUE)

Arguments

x

Numeric vector of the observations collected so far (at least 2).

A

The loss constant: the price of one unit of squared estimation error, in the same currency as c. A positive number.

c

The cost of sampling one observation. A positive number.

gamma

The positive constant of the correction term \(n^{-\gamma}\) in the stopping rule; default 1. See Details for the tradeoff. Use the same value in seq_mr_dfr_mean_arb_pilot.

na.rm

Logical; should NA values be removed first? Default TRUE. With FALSE, missing values are an error.

Value

An object of class c("smsd_check", "data.frame") with columns term and value and these rows:

mean

The sample mean, the point estimate.

risk

The estimated risk at the current sample size, \(A S_n^2/n + c\,n\).

optimal_n

The sample size the current data call for, \(\lceil (A/c)^{1/2}(S_n + n^{-\gamma}) \rceil\).

current_n

The number of observations used.

risk and optimal_n are NA when the data are constant. Attributes: is_satisfied (TRUE when current_n has reached optimal_n), current_n, criterion_n (equal to optimal_n), method, loss_A, cost_c, gamma, variance_unusable (TRUE when the data are constant, so that no variance has been estimated), and notes. conf_level and width are NULL.

Details

The function does not collect data and keeps no state. Call it after each new observation (or batch), starting once seq_mr_dfr_mean_arb_pilot observations are in hand, and stop sampling the first time attr(out, "is_satisfied") is TRUE.

The loss from estimating the mean \(\mu\) by the sample mean of \(n\) observations is \(A(\bar{X}_n - \mu)^2 + c\,n\): \(A\) prices a unit of squared estimation error and \(c\) is the cost of one observation. Its expectation for a fixed \(n\), the risk, is \(A\sigma^2/n + c\,n\) for any distribution with variance \(\sigma^2\); it is smallest at \(n^* = (A/c)^{1/2}\sigma\), where it equals \(2 c\,n^*\). Sampling stops at the first \(n\) (at or beyond the pilot size) with $$n \ge (A/c)^{1/2}\,(S_n + n^{-\gamma}),$$ where \(S_n\) is the sample standard deviation. The correction term \(n^{-\gamma}\) keeps the rule from being met on a standard deviation estimate that happens to be very small early on; it vanishes as the sample grows. The optimal_n row is the right hand side rounded up, and the risk row is the estimated risk at the current sample size, \(A S_n^2/n + c\,n\); both are evaluated at the current data.

The choice of gamma, and the units of the data. The correction term is added to a standard deviation, so it is in the units of the data, and the procedure depends on the units in which the data are recorded. It inflates the final sample size \(n\) by a factor of roughly \(1 + n^{-\gamma}/\sigma\): negligible when the standard deviation is 1 or more in the units of the data, and not negligible when it is much smaller unless gamma is large. A smaller gamma gives more protection against stopping too early at the price of more observations. Chattopadhyay and Kelley (2016, p. 636) use 0.49 for a correction of the same kind in their rule for the coefficient of variation, and note that a value above 1/2 falls outside part of their theory. The default here is 1 because it behaved well across scales in simulation, where 0.49 oversampled at small scales (see below).

The optimality is asymptotic. As the cost per observation falls (so that \(n^*\) grows), the expected final sample size approaches \(n^*\) and the risk approaches the minimum \(2 c\,n^*\). In simulation (exponential data, A = 100, c = 0.01, so that \(n^*\) is 100 times the standard deviation, the pilot of seq_mr_dfr_mean_arb_pilot() with matching gamma, 40,000 replications, Monte Carlo standard errors at most 0.004), with gamma = 1 the expected final sample size was 1.10, 0.99, and 0.99 times \(n^*\) at standard deviations of 0.25, 1, and 3, and the risk was 1.02, 1.02, and 1.01 times the minimum. With gamma = 0.49 the sample size ratios were 1.64, 1.08, and 1.01 and the risk ratios 1.13, 1.01, and 1.01.

Constant data. If every observation is equal, or equal up to rounding error (a range of no more than \(10^{-10}\) times the largest absolute value, as with gain scores of 0.3 computed as posttest minus pretest), the sample variance is zero, or nothing but rounding error, and under the rule as printed the correction term alone would eventually stop the sampling. The function departs from the printed rule deliberately: no variance has been estimated, so the rule is reported as not met, risk and optimal_n are NA, attr(out, "variance_unusable") is TRUE, and a note says so (see smsd_check_methods); data whose real spread is that small beside their size should have a common value subtracted first.

Extreme units. Data that do vary, but whose spread is so large or so small that the sample variance cannot be represented in double precision (differences among the observations beyond about \(10^{154}\) or below about \(10^{-162}\)), are an error that says to change the units. That case is not reported as a rule not yet met, because collecting more data cannot help.

References

Chattopadhyay, B., & Kelley, K. (2016). Estimation of the coefficient of variation with minimum risk: A sequential method for minimizing sampling error and study cost. Multivariate Behavioral Research, 51(5), 627–648. doi:10.1080/00273171.2016.1203279

Mukhopadhyay, N., & de Silva, B. M. (2009). Sequential methods and their applications. Chapman & Hall/CRC. ISBN:9780367386535

See also

seq_mr_dfr_mean_arb_pilot; seq_mr_norm_mean for the normal theory rule without the correction term; seq_mr_cv and seq_mr_smd for minimum risk estimation of effect sizes.

Other seq_mr_dfr_mean_arb: seq_mr_dfr_mean_arb_pilot()

Author

Bhargab Chattopadhyay bhargab@iiitvadodara.ac.in, Ken Kelley kkelley@nd.edu

Examples

# Mean order value for an online retailer, in dollars. An error of one
# dollar (squared) is worth 400 dollars and auditing one more order
# costs 0.25 dollars. Order values are right skewed; they are simulated
# here with a standard deviation of 10, so the best sample size is 400
# (the square root of 400 / 0.25, times 10).
set.seed(113)
m <- seq_mr_dfr_mean_arb_pilot(A = 400, c = 0.25)
orders <- rgamma(m, shape = 4, scale = 5)
out <- seq_mr_dfr_mean_arb(orders, A = 400, c = 0.25)
out
#> Sequential check (minimum risk point estimation (distribution free mean, arbitrary variance))
#> 
#>   Current n       : 7
#>   Criterion n     : 345
#> 
#>   mean              : 19.85849
#>   risk              : 4092.808
#>   optimal_n         : 345
#>   current_n         : 7
#> 
#>   Stopping rule met: FALSE

# Add one order at a time until the stopping rule is met.
while (!attr(out, "is_satisfied")) {
  orders <- c(orders, rgamma(1, shape = 4, scale = 5))
  out <- seq_mr_dfr_mean_arb(orders, A = 400, c = 0.25)
}
out
#> Sequential check (minimum risk point estimation (distribution free mean, arbitrary variance))
#> 
#>   Current n       : 401
#>   Criterion n     : 401
#> 
#>   mean              : 20.27692
#>   risk              : 200.2885
#>   optimal_n         : 401
#>   current_n         : 401
#> 
#>   Stopping rule met: TRUE
